0.text: roxy is a strict, programmable HTTP firewall. Every request and response streams through a pipeline you compose: addons that can rewrite, withhold, answer or block, then rules that judge exactly what they pass on. Run it as an egress proxy for a workload you don't trust, or as a gateway in front of the APIs your clients call. Every exchange takes the same path: roxy parses it, the addons see it, the rules judge it, and the connector dials the upstream (how roxy works). It fails closed: anything roxy cannot parse, verify or classify is denied.
0.title: Overview

1.text: Sandbox containment. An untrusted workload has no route out except through roxy. It points HTTPS_PROXY at roxy's proxy port and trusts roxy's CA; roxy decrypts each request, judges it, injects the credentials the workload never sees, and logs every decision. The network does the containing; roxy decides what gets out (sandbox containment). HTTP gateway. Clients address roxy directly, as anthropic.gw.example.com behind a load balancer that terminates TLS. Rules route each request by host and inject the real API keys, so clients hold placeholders; client authentication is an addon. It governs the traffic sent to it; it is not containment (HTTP gateway).

5.text: Run clients through roxy with three controls on every model call: a WASM addon that authenticates the client against an auth service, a WASM addon that holds each user to a token quota kept by a quota service, and an inspect_sentinel sidecar that blocks tool calls matching a denylist. roxy runs in node mode, leasing its policy and the model's API key from a minimal control plane and shipping its flow log back. 8.text: docker compose up --build --attach traffic The first run builds the images, which takes a few minutes. Eight containers start; only the last one's output is shown (Ctrl-C stops them): controlplane: enrols roxy, serves roxy.yaml and the model's API key as a one-minute lease, and prints the flow events roxy ships.roxy: the proxy on 127.0.0.1:3128, with the two addons at /etc/roxy/addons/. It has no config file; it runs the policy it leases.fake-model: answers POST /v1/messages from responses.json, one entry per call in order, streamed or whole, with the usage the real API sends. Each user has a bucket of 600 tokens that refills at five a second.sentinel: the inspect_sentinel sidecar, on a network with no route out.inspect-view: Inspect's log viewer.traffic: the clients. Alice calls every six seconds, bob every twenty, and mallory, whose credential is unknown, every thirty.
8.title: Start the stack

9.text: Each client is the Anthropic SDK, pointed at the model through roxy, with its credential in an x-roxy-auth header; each call is one streamed POST /v1/messages. The scripted responses go by: a greeting, a Bash tool call running ls -la, then one running curl, which comes back as traffic-1  | [alice #2] I will fetch that page for you. roxy's sentinel blocked a Bash tool call (denylist match: 'curl'). The sentinel took the tool call out before the client saw it and put a note in its place. Mallory is refused by the auth gate: traffic-1  | [mallory #1] 401 AuthenticationError: credential refused by the auth service Within the first minute alice drains her bucket, and her calls stop reaching the model until it refills: traffic-1  | [alice #8] 429 RateLimitError: token bucket empty (600 tokens, refills 5/s); try again in 15s

11.title: Watch it in Inspect View

12.text: docker compose logs roxy One line per request: the rule it matched, the addons it went through in order ("addons":["auth-gate","token-quota","sentinel"]), the user:alice tag the auth gate set, and the set_header:x-api-key mutation the rule made. The addons' own events are there too: endpoint_call for every call to the auth service and the quota board, layer_record for the verdicts and usage reports. Capture keeps whole requests and responses as well. The same events reach the control plane in batches, within the lease's five-second flush interval; docker compose logs controlplane shows each one prefixed with the node's id.
12.title: Read roxy's flow log

13.text: The lease is valid for sixty seconds and refreshed every fifteen. Stop the control plane: docker compose stop controlplane Within a minute every call fails with a 403 and roxy's /readyz answers 503 policy_expired: an unreachable control plane is not a reason to deny, but an expired lease is. docker compose start controlplane brings the next lease and roxy recovers without a restart. To revoke the node instead, add its id (the enrolled node-... line in the control plane's log) to the control plane's revoked file; the next poll answers 410 and roxy denies everything until it is re-enrolled: docker compose exec controlplane sh -c 'echo node-xxxxxx >> /data/revoked'
13.title: Let the lease run down

14.text: Ctrl-C in the terminal running up, then: docker compose down -v
14.title: Clean up

15.text: An exchange passes through the addons in the order roxy.yaml lists them, then the rules; each addon wraps everything below it. The auth gate (addons/auth-gate) reads the credential from x-roxy-auth, asks the auth service who it belongs to through a named endpoint, caches the answer in its state store under a hash of the credential, tags the flow user:alice, strips the header and passes the request on. A missing or refused credential is answered 401 and never leaves. The tag is how a layer hands an identity to the layers below; the rule injects the API key from a secret.The token quota (addons/token-quota) asks the quota board, before a model call leaves, whether the user's bucket holds anything (the user is the user: tag, or the client IP without one) and answers 429 with retry-after if not. Otherwise it reads input_tokens from message_start and output_tokens from message_delta as the response streams, changing nothing, and reports them when the stream ends or is cut off. Usage is known only after the response, so a user can overrun by one call and go into debt.The sentinel is a service layer: an out-of-process addon that each model call streams through over a WebSocket. It turns every tool call in a model response into an inspect_sentinel BeforeToolCall step and runs the configured sentinel on it. It sits below the quota layer, so what the quota layer meters is what the client got. Whatever any layer passes on, the rules judge again, and they allow exactly one request, POST /v1/messages on the model host. The rule's condition is the one the quota and the sentinel run on (a YAML anchor in roxy.yaml), so a request those layers skip, /v1/messages/ say, is one the rules deny rather than a model call that went unmetered and unjudged.
15.title: What just happened

16.text: roxy enrols once with a token, keeps the node token it is issued in its state dir, and polls the control plane for its lease: the whole roxy.yaml, the values of the secrets it declares as lease: true, and how to ship the flow log (node mode). controlplane/controlplane.py is the server side of the node protocol in one file. It turns model_key: { env: MODEL_API_KEY } into a lease secret from its own environment, and its lease_id is a hash of the config and secrets, so editing roxy.yaml changes the lease and roxy applies it on its next poll. Its enrolment token stays valid across restarts, because roxy's state dir is tmpfs and every docker compose up re-enrols; a real control plane consumes a token on first use. To run roxy from the file instead, with no control plane: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.standalone.yaml up --build --attach traffic
16.title: Node mode

17.text: A layer that cannot do its job (the auth service unreachable, the quota board answering something that is not an allowance, the sentinel unable to read a response) fails the exchange: roxy answers 503 naming the layer and logs a layer_error. The quota layer reads a non-streamed response whole to find its usage, and one over 8 MiB fails the same way; aborted streams are charged for the usage seen before the abort. Stop the quota board (docker compose stop quota-board) to see it.
17.title: Failure is closed

18.text: The sentinel runs deny_regex from policies.py, which searches <tool name> <arguments as JSON> for a regular expression. The default catches curl, wget, nc, ncat, ssh, scp, rsync and rm -rf. Set your own with SENTINEL_DENY: SENTINEL_DENY='\bls\b' docker compose up --attach traffic Any inspect_sentinel monitor or protocol works in its place: set SENTINEL to its module:attribute, and for one that asks a model, SENTINEL_MONITOR_MODEL and a route out (add the sentinel service to the egress network). The sidecar is in sentinel/.
18.title: The denylist

19.text:
Any HTTP client that honours HTTP_PROXY can take the clients' place; the proxy is on 127.0.0.1:3128. Claude Code, against the scripted model: HTTP_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:3128 \
ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://fake-model:8080 \
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=placeholder \
ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS='x-roxy-auth: alice-secret' \
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 \
claude To point the stack at the real API, allow api.anthropic.com in the rules, set the real key as the model_key secret, and trust roxy's CA (http://127.0.0.1:3130/roxy-ca.pem) in the client, since roxy then terminates TLS. The client follows HTTP_PROXY because it chooses to; any process can ignore it. To contain an agent, run it where its only route out is roxy (sandbox containment).

21.text:
Addons are listed under addons:, in the order they wrap the exchange
(addon model). Each entry is a WASM layer or a
service layer; the two kinds share most keys. addons:
  - name: sentinel
    kind: wasm
    path: /etc/roxy/addons/sentinel.wasm
    mode: enforce
    when: host == "api.anthropic.com" and path starts_with "/v1/messages"
    subscribe: { request: full, response: head }
    capabilities: [state, record, endpoints]
    endpoints:
      monitor-model:
        url: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
        headers: { x-api-key: "${secret:monitor_key}" }
        timeout: 10s
      threat-intel:
        url: https://ti.internal:8443/score
        path: prefix
        private_ok: true
    limits: { max_memory: 128mb, first_byte_timeout: 30s }
    config: { reject_at: 0.8 }

  - name: monitor
    kind: service
    endpoint: sidecar
    mode: observe
    sample: 0.1
    subscribe: { request: head, response: head }
    endpoints:
      sidecar: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:9000/layer", private_ok: true }
    limits: { first_byte_timeout: 2s, max_connections: 4, max_streams: 100 }

24.text:
Limits catch a broken layer, not a slow one: a slow layer makes its
exchanges slow, not denied, with one exception. Exchanges that keep every
instance busy past first_byte_timeout cost the exchanges queued behind
them, which are denied rather than wait (max_instances below). Each is
optional. keykinddefaultwhat it boundsfirst_byte_timeoutboth30show long a layer may hold a head, request or response, before passing it on or answering: its own time only (starting an instance, its work, endpoint calls, reading the body it was given), never time next spends below it. Overrun fails the layer closed (budget:first_byte_timeout for a WASM layer, service:timeout for a service layer), and the exchange with it in enforce mode. A service layer gets one budget to obtain a stream and a fresh one from each head; an observing one gets a last from roxy's final message to its own end of the stream. It bounds the layer's own time, not the exchange's: a layer that forwards a head and holds back the body keeps the upstream waiting for as long as it likes, with no clock running (service layers). It also bounds the wait for an instance when all max_instances are busy, on its own: an enforce exchange that gets none within it is denied (layer_error, no_instance); an observer loses its copy (observer_lagged, no_instance)max_memorywasm64mblinear memory per instance, summed over the instance's memories; table growth and the host resource table (4096 live resources: body streams, pollables, pending responses) are capped too. What a layer holds of a body lives here. An interpreter in WASM (Python) needs 128–256 MiBmax_instanceswasm1024live instances, so concurrent exchanges and, with max_memory, the layer's memory. An exchange that finds none free waits first_byte_timeout for one, then fails closed (no_instance), so the clients holding every instance cannot queue the rest indefinitely. Instances start on demandrecycle_after_exchangeswasm10000an instance is replaced after this many exchanges; 0 replaces it after every exchangerecycle_above_memorywasmthree quarters of max_memoryan instance whose memory passed this is replaced after its exchange. it takes (a WebSocket for as long as the relay's idle timeout allows); the
client's and upstream's idle timeouts still apply. CPU has no limit: a
guest yields to the runtime on a 1 ms engine-wide tick, so it never stalls
a worker thread and cancellation takes effect within a tick.

A layer has no access outside its own streams. capabilities grants it

27.title: Capabilities

28.text:
subscribe names what the layer gets of each direction. With full (the
default) the layer owns that direction: it reads the body, chunk by chunk,
and what it passes on is the body that goes on. With head the layer gets
the head with an empty body and no content-length, and the body bypasses
it: whatever the layer passes on (the head it gives next, or the head it
answers with) carries the body it did not see, spliced on by roxy, with
the framing roxy knows. An enforce layer can still deny, rewrite or answer at a head it is
subscribed to; the bodies stream past it at no cost in copies or
buffering.A response head-only layer answers with the status it was given to pass
the response on with its head edited; the body from below follows. Any
other status is an answer of the layer's own: its body stands and the
body from below is dropped, so a layer can refuse at the response head.
A layer that answers without next resolving answers whole too, since
there is no body from below.A layer that passes on bytes of a body it is not subscribed to fails the
exchange closed: a 503 before the response head, a cut body after it,
layer_error with kind: unsubscribed:request or
unsubscribed:response. The bypassed body keeps its framing when the
layer's own body for that direction is complete as the two are joined,
which is always for a service layer (its head-only direction is a head
and an end with nothing between) and for a WASM layer when next is
given an empty bytes body; joined to one still open (a WASM layer's
streamed next body, or any WASM response body, whose end waits for the
handler) it goes out without a content-length, chunked on HTTP/1.1, so
a cut is visible however the bytes interleave.A head-only observer gets copies of the heads and no copy of the body,
so neither the lag budget nor the buffer budget is touched for it.The rules are not affected: they judge the request that leaves the
stack, head and body, whoever supplied each.Bodies are decoded for the layers, and a WebSocket relayed without
extensions, only when some layer that runs is subscribed to a body
(content codings, WebSockets).
28.title: What a layer sees

29.text:
when is a rule language condition over admission
fields. A layer runs only on the exchanges it matches; the rest pass it at
no cost (no instance, no body pumping, no service session). when sees the request as it reaches the layer: what the layer above
passed on, re-validated. A layer above can steer a request into or out of
a lower layer's when.It may read admission fields, headers, the query, state[..], metric.<id>
and address lists. body.*, response.* and ws.* are config errors.tag["x"] sees tags set by enforce layers above, not the rules' tags
(the rules run below the stack).An unavailable input (a metric, an address list, a missing value under an
operator that cannot answer for null) fails the flow closed like a
layer failure (503, layer_error with kind: when:<code>), never
skips the layer. On an observe layer the failure is logged and the layer
gets no copy.A layer when skipped on a WebSocket's upgrade request is not in that
WebSocket's byte path. sample (observe only) is drawn from the flow id, so it is the same for a
flow however often it is asked.
29.title: Choosing exchanges

30.text:
The stack sits in the exchange core both fronts share: the front drives
the client's request body into the first layer, and the last layer's
next runs the rules, the upstream, then the in-flight rules on the
response. What a layer passes on is re-validated as strictly as a client request:
an absolute http(s) URI; host, hop-by-hop and framing fields refused
at the boundary (roxy derives them); the workload's limits applied. A
WASM layer may not set content-length either (the body carries its own
length); a service layer may, and the body it sends is held to it
(service layers). chain.next
fills in the scheme and authority from the exchange when the layer
leaves them unset.A layer's answer must be a final response; a 1xx other than the 101
of a relayed upgrade fails closed as invalid_response.A layer's response body to the client waits for the flow log like every
forwarded body (audit backpressure).Layers compile at config load and are cached across reloads while their
file and settings are unchanged, so instance pools stay warm. A reload
swaps the stack for new exchanges; exchanges in flight finish on theirs. In the flow log: fieldwith addonsaddonsthe layers that ran, in stack order; a layer its when or sample skipped is not in itrules, decision, terminal_rulethe rules' decision on the request that left the stack; req is what the client sent. Metric keys (for the rules' samples and metric-get) also come from the request that left. A layer whose next returned the rules' 403 and then answered 200 itself is logged decision: deny, res.status: 200decision: answered, terminal_rule: layer:<name>a layer answered itself, whatever its status: the outermost layer that did not pass on the response from below (it never called next, or answered while next was pending, failed or dropped). If its request had already left, the forwarded request is abandoned (its body cut, never ended as complete) and the record keeps what the rules decided and the bytes sent, with reason: upstream_aborted503, terminal_rule: layer:<name>, reason: layer_errora layer failed before the response head; the connection is closed and a layer_error event follows with kind one of trap, budget:<limit>, capability:<name>, invalid_request, invalid_response, no_response, unsubscribed:<direction>, ... After the head, the body is cut (HTTP/1.1 breaks the connection, HTTP/2 resets the stream) and layer_error follows. Which layer, if any, is one rule (who is blamed)
30.title: In the proxy

31.text:
On a flow some layer runs on and is subscribed to the body, roxy decodes
the client's request body as the first such layer gets it and the response
before it reaches the innermost such layer, removing content-encoding;
the body's length becomes unknown. A body no running layer is subscribed
to is not decoded, and reaches the upstream or the client as sent. The client gets an uncompressed response and the upstream an
uncompressed request body; the origin's response to roxy stays
compressed. Nothing re-encodes.The codings and their strictness are the rules'
(HTTP). Data that does not decode, or
a decoded body over limits.max_request_body_bytes or
limits.max_response_body_bytes, cuts the exchange like any failed body,
also on a flow only an observer runs on.A body in a coding roxy does not know passes through as it is, with its
content-encoding; so does a 206 or any response with content-range.The rules below the stack read the response before any layer and decode
it for themselves (body rules).No extension (permessage-deflate above all) is negotiated on a
WebSocket a body-subscribed layer runs on (WebSockets). http.decode_for_addons: false turns this off: layers see the bytes as
sent, with their content-encoding, and WebSockets negotiate whatever
extensions client and upstream agree on.
31.title: Content codings

32.text:
A layer gets the upgrade request in handle and passes it on with next
(a service layer forwards it on its stream); the response from below is the
101. After it, the request body carries the client's bytes and the
response body the upstream's for as long as the WebSocket is open. A layer
reads, rewrites or holds back either direction as any body, refuses the
upgrade by answering without next, and is left out of the WebSocket when
its when skips the upgrade request. A subscription to one body puts the
layer in that direction only: the other's bytes flow past it, however long
its handler lives on relaying the direction it is in. A layer that turns the upstream's 101 into another status fails the
exchange closed (503 from layer:<name>) and roxy closes the upstream
WebSocket; a 101 with no upgrade from below fails closed too.Only Upgrade: websocket is an upgrade for the layers. A request asking
for any other upgrade (h2c, say) is an ordinary request roxy forwards
once it strips the upgrade, with its body and the usual body cap.The bodies carry raw WebSocket frames. Frames from the client are masked,
so their payload reads as sent only from the upstream's side.A layer must stream both bodies at once: the request body ends only when
the client closes, while the response streams all along (the
roxy-addon SDK does this). Holding bytes back until more arrive stalls
an interactive protocol.No clock runs on the bodies. When the relay ends, roxy closes the
client's connection whether or not the layers have ended their bodies;
bytes already on their way get a second to arrive.
32.title: WebSockets

33.text:
Every failure is closed. A trap, an exceeded budget, a second next
or respond, a missing capability, a host failure, a head the host
refuses, a body stream that is not the host's, a missing response, bytes
on an unsubscribed body, a handler that returns still holding a body
stream or a pending response, or a cancelled exchange is a
LayerError: a deny, or a cut exchange after the response head.A client that gives up cancels the exchange. The guest is stopped,
its instance discarded, the slot freed. No layer_error is logged.No clean end for a failed body. A guest body ends with an error once
its exchange has failed; a response body the guest produces (bytes or a
stream) holds its end until the handler returns, so a trap after the last
byte still cuts it. An empty body, or a passed-through body of known
length, goes out with content-length and is complete once sent. A streamed body is
complete only through finish: dropped unfinished, it is cut, and a
response body dropped unfinished fails the exchange.An abandoned request is cut, not failed. A request body passed to
next that the guest drops without finish is cut at the upstream. If
the guest is still waiting on next's response, the layer has failed
(invalid_request); if it has dropped the pending response or already
has the response, it may answer itself and its answer stands. A body the

35.title: Address floor

36.text:
Named CIDR sets, used as an unconditional deny floor (upstream.deny_lists)
and as @name in rules. address_lists:
  - name: blocked
    file: /etc/roxy/lists/blocked.txt    # one IPv4/IPv6 CIDR or address per line; `#` comments
  - name: cloud-metadata
    inline: [169.254.169.254/32, "fd00:ec2::254/128", 100.100.100.200/32] Representation. Two sorted tables of disjoint CIDR blocks per list,
one per family, binary-searched: 8 bytes per IPv4 block, 32 per IPv6, no
allocation per lookup (a million IPv4 plus 100k IPv6 entries: about
11 MiB, tens of nanoseconds). Nested and duplicate entries merge. A
malformed line is an error naming file and line; a malformed inline entry
is reported at address_lists[i].inline[j]. A file over
limits.max_address_list_bytes (256 MiB), or not valid UTF-8, is a load
error.Matching. The deny floor matches every form
(above), since matching more
is the safe direction for a deny. Rule membership (ip
in @list) is exact, with only the IPv4-mapped equivalence, since a rule
may allow on it: client.ip in @internal must not treat a 6to4 address
embedding an internal IPv4 address as internal.In rules. @name works wherever a CIDR does: right of in / not
in with an ip field. An undefined list is a compile error.Reload. List files are watched with the config. A changed file is
recompiled and swapped with the policy, and upstream pools are flushed,
so a pooled connection to a newly denied IP is never reused. An exchange
in flight keeps its policy, pools and lists, and can still open a
connection the new lists would deny; the next exchange on the connection
uses the new lists.roxy check reports each list's entry count. roxy rule test loads
lists as roxy run would; if one fails to load it warns and treats every
@list as unavailable, so a rule reading one fails closed.

Every injected secret value is scrubbed from any logged string, the

48.title: Redaction

49.text:
The write path never drops a record while roxy runs
(audit backpressure). One writer per destination. Emitters serialise each event on their
own thread and enqueue the bytes; one writer thread owns the file and
writes everything queued in one batch. The writer waits a moment for
more records before each write, so a burst is one write and a record is
written within a couple of milliseconds of being emitted.Backpressure. Emitting never blocks or drops. Once unwritten bytes
pass log.flow.high_water (8 MiB) the log reports not ready and every
traffic producer waits for it: each new client connection, exchange and
HTTP/2 stream, each forwarded body chunk and each WebSocket read. A
failing destination (disk full, I/O error) holds traffic the same way, and
is reported.Rotation happens at a batch boundary, so a record never spans two
files: the file is renamed to <path>.<UTC timestamp>-<seq>, a new one
is opened, files beyond max_files are deleted (oldest first), and
rotated files are optionally gzipped in the background. Names sort in
rotation order even across a restart on a clock behind the previous run's:
a rotation on a clock behind the newest existing name reuses its stamp
with a higher sequence. Only files of that name shape count towards
max_files or are deleted. A
failed rotation is a failed write: traffic is held and it is retried.
SIGHUP reopens the file, for external rotation.Shutdown. Everything queued is written before exit, with up to 10
seconds of retries for a failing destination; whatever is still unwritten
when roxy then exits is lost, and an error logged. This is the one point
at which a record can be dropped.Durability. Each batch is flushed to the operating system, and
max_file_bytes checked, at the batch boundary. roxy does not fsync: a
roxy crash loses nothing queued; a kernel crash or power loss can lose
batches the OS had not yet written to disk. log:
  redact_headers: []
  flow:
    path: /var/log/roxy/flow.jsonl  # absent = stdout
    connection_events: false
    ws_message_every: 0             # also log every Nth WebSocket message; 0 = denied only
    high_water: 8mb                 # at least 64kb
    max_file_bytes: 100mb           # absent = never rotate; at least 4kb
    max_files: 10                   # absent = keep all; at least 1
    compress: true roxy check refuses max_file_bytes, max_files or compress without
path (stdout cannot rotate), and max_files or compress without
max_file_bytes. The same floors apply under log.capture. roxy's own operational logs go to stderr through tracing: --log-format
json|pretty and --log-level (or RUST_LOG).
49.title: Writing

50.text:
roxy tees the heads and bodies of exchanges, exactly as forwarded, to
<capture_dir>/capture.rxc: those an admission rule selects with capture:
request | response | both, or every forwarded exchange with
log.capture.all: true. Capture is decided at admission and covers
the exchange from its first byte; the taps sit after the in-flight rules
allowed a chunk. WebSocket relays are captured both ways at the relay next
to the upstream, not as an addon layer changes them for the client. Capture is written like the flow log (one writer, batching, rotation,
backpressure). Injected secret values are scrubbed from every string of a
captured head (URL, header names and values); nothing else is: the
header-name redaction above is flow-log only, and bodies are captured
unredacted. capture_dir: /var/lib/roxy/capture   # absent = capture disabled; restart to change
log:
  capture:
    all: false
    high_water: 64mb
    max_file_bytes: 1gb
    max_files: 20
    compress: true
limits:
  max_capture_body_bytes: 16mb       # per direction per exchange Every log.capture setting needs capture_dir; roxy check reports
settings given without it.
50.title: Capture

51.title: Capture format

52.text:
Everything a layer can do outside its own streams, each a capability
granted in config
(capabilities). A WASM
layer calls them as the flow and endpoints imports named here; a
service layer sends the matching messages on its stream
(service layers), except
endpoints.call, which a service does for itself. Both reach one host, so
a call means the same and fails the same way for either kind. The caps on
each (payload sizes, calls in flight, key length) are in
fixed caps.
52.title: Host services

53.text:
endpoints.call(name, head, body): roxy resolves the name to the configured
URL, attaches the endpoint's headers (replacing any the layer set), applies
the timeout, and enforces the address floor and deny lists. The
layer cannot name a destination and never sees the credentials. Calls do not
pass through the layer stack, so a monitor's own model call cannot recurse
through it; the response goes back to the layer, not through the rules. Each call emits an endpoint_call flow event. An exchange has at most 8 calls in flight. A further endpoints.call
waits for one of them to be answered before it returns, and before roxy
takes the call's body: a waiting call holds nothing.The request body is buffered before the call (at most 16 MiB), and
reading it counts against the timeout.An unknown name, a denied address, a refused path, a timeout and a
failure reach the layer as distinct error variants
(destination-not-found, destination-denied, request-uri-invalid,
timeout, internal), through the pending-response the call returns. The endpoint's path setting: pathtargetfixed (default)the configured URL is the whole target; the request's path and query are ignoredprefixthe request's path, normalised (percent-encodings canonicalised, . segments removed), is appended under the configured path; its query follows the endpoint's own. A percent-encoded slash or backslash (%2F, %5C) is refused A segment that starts with .., in any percent-encoded spelling and
whatever follows the dots (..;x, which an origin that strips path
parameters reads as ..), is refused in both modes: the call fails with
request-uri-invalid, nothing is dialled, and the endpoint_call
event records the refusal. Under prefix, text a layer
reflects into the path can pick any route below the configured path, with
roxy's credential attached.
53.title: Endpoints (endpoints)

54.text:
flow.state-get / flow.state-put: the state store
the rules read as state["key"] and write with set_state. A key a layer
writes is the key a rule reads, so a layer can leave a mark for a rule to
deny on, and read what a rule left. Values are strings; a layer that wants
state["k"] == "yes" to match writes yes. A state-put without a TTL
gets the store's default (one hour). A miss returns none. A key over
1 KiB or a value over 64 KiB returns an error to the layer. A write when
the store is full fails the exchange closed, as it does a rule's
set_state; nothing is evicted. Only an enforce layer may write: a
state-put from an observer fails the layer (layer_error, kind host)
and the exchange goes on, like add-tag, since the store steers every
flow's rules. The store survives a reload, under
limits.max_state_entries.
54.title: State (state)

55.text:
flow.current(): the flow id, connection id, tags, and the principal as
roxy established it (client IP, listener, TLS SNI). Key per-principal state
on these, not on client-supplied session headers. flow.config() is the
layer's config: value as a JSON document. A service gets both in its
open message.
55.title: Identity and config

56.text:
flow.record(kind, json) writes a layer_record event to the flow
log with the flow id, layer name and timestamp. kind and every string
value in the document pass through the secret redactor; a document that
is not JSON fails the exchange. The call
waits while the flow log is behind and is never dropped.
56.title: Record (record)

57.text:
flow.metric-get(id, []) reads a metric for this flow's own key (the key
fields evaluated on the request that left the addon stack); explicit key
values are refused. A key with no entry reads none (a rule reads the same
key as 0); an unknown id, or a key field the request does not have, fails
the exchange. flow.log writes to roxy's operational log with the
flow id and layer name.
57.title: Metrics and log (metrics, log)

58.text:
flow.quarantine() puts the whole proxy into
quarantine: the exchange it was called on
is refused _quarantined (nothing of it is forwarded, whatever the layer
answers), and so is every exchange after it, until an operator or the
control plane lifts it. It is for what a layer is sure must stop the
workload; one bad request is denied by answering it. Only an enforce layer
may call it: from an observer it fails the layer (layer_error, kind
host) and the exchange goes on, like add-tag. The
quarantined flow event's cause is kind: layer with the layer's name and
the flow. A config whose layers hold the capability needs roxy run
--state-dir, as one with a quarantine rule does. A layer cannot
terminate a client: it denies the exchange.
58.title: Quarantine (quarantine)

59.text:
Every limit resolves in the closed direction: an error anywhere between
accept and the upstream connect produces a deny response or a closed socket
(fail closed).

61.text:

61.title: Limits

62.text:
The timeouts are permissive by default: roxy decides what passes, not how
long a well-behaved exchange may take, and a model call with minutes to its
first byte, a quiet WebSocket or a stream with long gaps should not hit one
unless the operator chose it. Only header_timeout is tight. Memory is
bounded by the buffer budget and the per-connection caps, not by the
timeouts, so a long timeout costs only the idle connection it keeps: timeouta long value holdsheader_timeouta connection slot (one of max_connections, or of the ca_server cap) and its socket, with no request to show for itbody_idle_timeouta connection slot and the exchange's buffers (its reservations under max_buffered_bytes, and up to 4 MiB of HTTP/2 receive window) while the client is silentidle_timeouta connection slot and its socket between requests, or a relayed WebSocket's two sockets and its reserved message buffers while nothing is sentresponse_header_timeouta connection slot, the upstream connection, and the exchange's buffers while the upstream thinksresponse_body_idle_timeoutthe same as above while the upstream pauses mid-body Tightening one trades those idle connections for cut exchanges; raise
max_connections instead if idle connections are what runs out.
62.title: Timeouts

63.text:
max_buffered_bytes bounds every buffer roxy holds for an exchange, in
aggregate. An exchange reserves before it fills a buffer; a reservation the
budget cannot cover fails at once, with no waiting and no eviction (503,
_fail_closed, buffer_budget_exhausted). This is the whole list of what
is charged: bufferreservationa body a rule reads (body.text, response.body.text)max_inspect_body_bytes, or its content-length if smaller; a body with a content-encoding reserves the whole cap, whatever its length, since its decoded size is not known until it is; nothing for a body known to be empty (no request body, a HEAD response, a 1xx, 204 or 304). Once buffered, it shrinks to what is held (the body as sent with its trailers, or its decoded text if larger) and stays until the exchange ends. A body over the cap holds only what was read before that was known: nothing when its content-length said so, the prefix read when it was found out mid-streama content decodereach decoder's window, charged before the decoder is created: 32 KiB for gzip or deflate, the window a br stream's first byte declares (1 KiB to 16 MiB), 8 MiB for zstd (the largest window accepted, which each frame may use). Stacked codings add up. Held while the decoder runs: for the rule's decision on an inspected body, for the whole body when it is decoded for the addon stack (http.decode_for_addons). A window the budget cannot cover fails closed before it is allocateda request body hashed for sign: aws_sigv4its content-length (at most max_sign_body_bytes) up front; a chunked body reserves chunk by chunk up to that cap and is refused at the chunk the budget cannot cover. Held until the exchange ends. unsigned_payload: true reserves nothing (signing AWS requests)an endpoint call's request bodywhat the guest sends, frame by frame as it is read (at most 16 MiB), held until the call is answered. A body the budget cannot cover refuses the call (host services)a WebSocket whose messages rules readtwice max_ws_message_bytes at the upgrade, held for the session. Reading bodies but not messages holds nothing for a WebSocketan observer's copythe bytes queued and not yet read, frame by frame, given back as the observer reads them (or drops the copy). A copy whose next frame would overrun the budget is cut (observer_lagged, reason: buffer_budget_exhausted): the budget bounds how far behind observers are in total, not how many exchanges are observed. A copy whose observer gets no instance within its first_byte_timeout is dropped the same way (reason: no_instance), so a busy observer cannot pin budget that enforce flows need Bytes in flight on a transport are bounded per connection rather than by
the budget: an HTTP/2 connection's receive window (connections),
the 256 KiB credit each body of a service layer
stream has, and the codec's parse buffers (max_header_bytes). Budget ÷ cap is how many exchanges can hold a buffer at once (defaults:
1024 bodies of unknown length under inspection, 32 WebSockets with message
rules, 1 GiB of unread observer copy). It must be at least the largest
single reservation.
63.title: Buffer budget

64.title: Reload

65.text:
A connection over max_connections or max_connections_per_client is
accepted and closed at once, with a connection_refused event. The
per-client cap counts TCP peers: it is applied when the connection is
accepted, before any X-Forwarded-For is read, so a listener's
forwarded_for does not change what it counts. The ca_server listener counts separately, max_connections in
total with no per-client cap, and logs its refusals to roxy's own log
rather than the flow log. A client that fills it starves the health
probes, so that port should not be reachable by untrusted clients.Every read is bounded (head size, body size, ClientHello size) and every
stage has a timeout. Nothing is allocated in proportion to an
attacker-supplied number before it is validated (content-length: 10^18
does not pre-allocate).Request bytes in flight on an HTTP/2 connection (sent by the client, not
yet taken by the upstream) sit outside max_buffered_bytes: the
connection's receive window caps them at 4 MiB, so one client IP can hold
at most max_connections_per_client × 4 MiB. Omitted, it is whatever
max_connections is, so behind a load balancer (one source IP for every
client, whatever forwarded_for resolves) the cap is the fleet's; lower
it on a proxy port where each client has its own address.Upstream connections are bounded by the clients: HTTP/1.1 origins get
one connection per concurrent request, HTTP/2 origins at most
upstream.max_h2_connections_per_origin (4 by default), each with an
8 MiB receive window (upstream).Bounded policy tables (metrics, state) never evict
(never evict).The proxy port serves only proxy semantics and roxy.internal; health
and CA download live on the separate ca_server listener, with a cap of
its own, so the two hold at most 2 × max_connections connection slots
between them.A panic in a connection task closes that connection only.On SIGTERM or Ctrl-C roxy stops accepting, drains exchanges in flight
for up to 10 seconds, and flushes the flow log and capture before
exiting.
65.title: Connections

66.text:
How clients talk to roxy, how requests are parsed and canonicalised, and
what goes to the upstream and back.
66.title: HTTP

67.text:
modethe client speaksrequest targethttp_proxy (default)HTTP/1.1 to a proxy (HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY)absolute-form, or CONNECT and then origin-form inside the tunnelhttpplain HTTP/1.1 to roxy as if it were the serverorigin-form; Host names the target Each mode accepts one protocol and closes anything else. roxy does not
authenticate clients; rules see listener.name and client.ip. listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy           # the default
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
    quarantine_on:             # optional; off when absent
      parse_errors: { count: 20, window: 1m }
  - name: gateway
    mode: http
    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
    forwarded_for:             # optional; without it X-Forwarded-For is ignored
      trusted_hops: 1          # the proxies in front of roxy: here, one load balancer quarantine_on.parse_errors puts the whole process into
quarantine once the listener has logged

number of seconds, at least 1s). It counts a client sending what roxy will not parse, not one that
is slow or leaves. Setting it needs roxy run --state-dir. forwarded_for.trusted_hops (at least 1; mode: http only) names the
client from X-Forwarded-For (below).
67.title: Listener modes

68.text:
Absolute-form (GET http://host/path HTTP/1.1): plain HTTP; Host
must equal the URI authority.CONNECT: a tunnel roxy inspects (below).Origin-form: rejected, except to roxy.internal, which serves the CA
certificate at /roxy-ca.pem
(CA distribution) and 404
for anything else.Proxy-Authorization is hop-by-hop: dropped, never forwarded.
68.title: HTTP proxy

69.text:
For a gateway behind a TLS-terminating load balancer
(HTTP gateway). Only origin-form. Absolute-form, CONNECT and * are refused
(target_form_mismatch; bad_request_target for *) and the connection
closed.The target is Host: required, exactly one (missing_host,
multiple_host, bad_authority), port 80 unless given, scheme http.
Hosts may differ between requests on one connection.Without a redirect the upstream is the Host authority over plain
HTTP; redirect with scheme: https sends it on over TLS.roxy.internal is a host like any other.A TLS handshake is closed at the record header (tls_on_http_listener).
69.title: HTTP listener

70.text:
Without forwarded_for, client.ip is the TCP peer: behind a load
balancer, the load balancer. With forwarded_for.trusted_hops: N, each of
the N proxies in front of roxy is taken to append the address it accepted
the connection from to X-Forwarded-For, so the client is the Nth entry
from the right of the header (every X-Forwarded-For line joined in
order). Entries to its left are the client's own and are never read. That address is client.ip in rules, metric keys and the flow log, and
the addon principal's client_ip: roxy has one notion of the client.
The flow log keeps the TCP peer as client.peer for forensics
(flow log).Each request is resolved on its own: a kept-alive connection from a load
balancer carries many clients.A request with fewer entries than hops, a trusted entry that is not a
bare IPv4 or IPv6 address (a port, brackets, a zone, unknown, an
obfuscated identifier), or a header over 4 KiB in all is refused as a
request roxy cannot parse: 400, reason forwarded_for_invalid, the
connection closed, counted by quarantine_on.parse_errors. It is never
attributed to the peer: a bypassed or misconfigured load balancer must
neither let a client choose its address nor fold every client into one.An IPv4-mapped IPv6 entry (::ffff:a.b.c.d) is the IPv4 address it
embeds, as a host literal is.The header goes upstream as received; roxy neither appends the peer nor
strips it.limits.max_connections_per_client is applied when the connection is
accepted, before any header, so it counts the peer
(limits). A hop count says how the header was built; it does not prove a connection
came through those proxies. A client that can reach the listener directly
can write N well-formed entries and choose its client.ip, so the
listener must be reachable only from the trusted proxies, which is the
network's claim to make (a security group, a private subnet), as
containment is (threat model). The setting is refused on an http_proxy listener: the requests inside a
CONNECT tunnel carry whatever X-Forwarded-For the client wrote, and no
proxy in front of roxy can add to them.
70.title: Clients behind a load balancer

71.text:
A CONNECT gets 200 Connection Established; decisions are made on the
requests inside the tunnel. The tunnel's first bytes must be: A TLS ClientHello
(ClientHello sniffing). With
tls.require_sni_match (default true) the SNI must name the CONNECT host,
compared canonicalised (sni_mismatch); an unusable SNI is closed
(bad_sni); no SNI means the CONNECT host. roxy terminates TLS with a
leaf for that host; the inner protocol is HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 by ALPN.Plaintext HTTP, only with http.allow_plain_in_connect (default
false). Anything else is closed; raw TCP never passes. Inside a tunnel, requests
are origin-form and their Host (or :authority) must match the CONNECT
host, port-normalised, whatever the SNI said.
71.title: CONNECT

72.text:
Inside a TLS tunnel, by ALPN (http.enable_h2, default true). The h2
crate parses it; the same semantic validation as HTTP/1.1 follows
(HTTP/2 requests). Upstream, roxy offers
h2 and http/1.1 and serialises as whichever the origin negotiates: the
canonical authority goes out as host over HTTP/1.1 and as :authority
alone over HTTP/2, never both. WebSocket upgrades always use HTTP/1.1
(WebSockets).
72.title: HTTP/2

73.text:
Two settings, one per direction. http.allow_response_trailers (default
true) forwards an origin's response trailers to the client, as HTTP/2
trailers or as the trailer section of a chunked HTTP/1.1 response (a
response with a declared length cannot carry them). gRPC, which puts the
call's outcome in grpc-status, works by default.
http.allow_request_trailers (default false) accepts trailers on requests,
HTTP/2 trailers or a chunked trailer section; without it a request that
carries them is refused with reason trailers. Request trailers arrive
after the rules have decided, so they stay opt-in. In either direction a
trailer section may not carry framing, routing, authentication or
content-* fields (authorization, cookie, set-cookie, range,
max-forwards, cache-control, every hop-by-hop name): on a request that
is a rejection, on a response the body is cut before the client sees it
complete. A body a rule or addon buffers to read keeps its trailers. Request trailers reach an origin only over h2: HTTP/1.1 needs the names
in a Trailer header before the body. Trailers to an HTTP/1.1 origin fail
with reason trailers (400 and close on HTTP/1.1, a stream reset on
HTTP/2) before the origin sees the request complete, for as long as any
HTTP/1.1 connection to that origin is open or pooled (hyper keeps idle
connections about 90 s), including one opened for a request held to
HTTP/1.1.
73.title: Trailers

74.text:
The client-facing HTTP/1.1 codec is roxy's own (on httparse for
tokenising): ambiguities RFC 9112 lets a server resolve are rejected. pub struct CanonicalRequest {
    pub method: Method,        // validated token
    pub scheme: Scheme,        // Http | Https
    pub authority: Authority,  // host (DNS name | IPv4 | IPv6), port always explicit
    pub path: Path,            // normalised, see below
    pub query: Option<Query>,  // validated raw bytes, parsed pairs for matching
    pub headers: Headers,      // lowercase names, ordered, validated, hop-by-hop removed
    pub body: Body,            // a stream; its known length, if any, decides upstream framing
    pub meta: RequestMeta,     // client version, receipt time, head size, target form, expect/upgrade
}
74.title: Canonical request

75.text:
A violation closes the connection, not just the request, and emits a
parse_error flow event with a stable reason code. The knobs live under
http: and default to strict. The header and body rules are one implementation, applied to every request
roxy judges: an HTTP/1.1 head, an HTTP/2 stream, and what a service layer
passes on. Each path adds only its own wire rules ahead of them (line
structure for HTTP/1.1, pseudo-headers and connection-specific fields for
HTTP/2, the fields a layer may not set), so a field list one path refuses
the others refuse for the same reason.
75.title: Rejection rules

76.text:
The method is a token of at most 32 bytes.The target form fits the context: absolute-form on the proxy port,
origin-form in a tunnel or on an http listener, authority-form only for
CONNECT on the proxy port.The version is exactly HTTP/1.1. HTTP/1.0 needs http.allow_http10
and its connection closes after the response whatever Connection says;
HTTP/0.9 is never accepted. A response of unknown length to an HTTP/1.0
client is close-delimited: the body ends when roxy closes the connection.
If the upstream body is cut short (upstream error, size cap, timeout,
forbidden trailer) roxy closes the connection all the same, so the client
cannot tell a cut body from a complete one. roxy still logs the failure.Lines end in CRLF; a bare LF or CR anywhere in the head is rejected.Head at most limits.max_header_bytes (64 KiB); URL at most
limits.max_url_bytes (8 KiB).
76.title: Request line

77.text:
Names are tokens, no whitespace before the colon, no obs-fold.Values are visible ASCII, SP and HTAB, surrounding whitespace stripped.
CR, LF, NUL and other controls are rejected; non-ASCII needs
http.allow_obs_text, under which the rules read each such byte as the
ISO-8859-1 character of the same value
(comparison).At most limits.max_headers (100) fields.Exactly one Host, matching the URI authority (absolute-form) or the
CONNECT host (tunnel); on an http listener it names the target. An
HTTP/1.0 absolute-form request may omit it.A host is a DNS name of A-labels, a strict dotted-quad IPv4 literal or a
bracketed IPv6 literal. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 literal ([::ffff:a.b.c.d])
is the IPv4 address it embeds and is parsed, matched, logged and
forwarded as a.b.c.d.At most one Content-Length, digits only, at most 19 digits; a duplicate
is rejected even with equal values. A non-zero length declared for a body
that has already ended (a layer passing content-length with an empty
body) is bad_content_length, not an empty body.Transfer-Encoding, if present, is exactly chunked: one field, one
value, no parameters, no other codings; rejected together with
Content-Length.GET, HEAD, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE carry a body only with
http.allow_body_on_get: without it, Transfer-Encoding: chunked or a
Content-Length above zero on those methods is rejected
(body_on_bodiless_method), whatever the body turns out to hold. CONNECT
never carries a body.Expect may only be 100-continue; anything else gets 417. roxy sends
100 Continue once the rules allow the request; when a rule reads the
request body it goes out before the body is judged, and a deny follows
the body.On a listener with forwarded_for, X-Forwarded-For must name the
client at the trusted hop
(forwarded_for_invalid; clients behind a load balancer).Hop-by-hop fields (Connection and every field it names, Keep-Alive,
Proxy-Connection, Proxy-Authorization, Proxy-Authenticate, TE,
Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade) are consumed and never
forwarded.
Upgrade is honoured only for a WebSocket a rule allows.
77.title: Headers

78.text:
Chunk sizes are hex, at most 16 digits. Chunk extensions need
http.allow_chunk_extensions, and with them the whole chunk-size line is
at most 4096 bytes; trailers need http.allow_request_trailers
and an h2 origin (trailers). The final CRLF
is enforced.At most limits.max_request_body_bytes (1 GiB), enforced while
streaming: exceeding it closes the connection mid-stream.The first request head on a connection must arrive within
limits.header_timeout (10 s) of the connection opening; every later
head within header_timeout of its first byte, pipelined bytes included.
In a tunnel each step gets its own header_timeout: the CONNECT head,
the first bytes that say whether the tunnel carries TLS, the client TLS
handshake, then the first request head (on HTTP/2, the handshake and
then the first stream). The body may not stall longer than limits.body_idle_timeout (10 m), which also
bounds how long the client may go without taking the next part of the
response (on HTTP/2: stream reset with CANCEL, response_error, reason
client_stalled).A client that closes while roxy still waits for the response ends the
exchange; nothing is written back; reason client_gone.
78.title: Body

79.text:
Pseudo-headers (:method, :scheme, :authority, :path) exactly once
each, before regular headers.Connection-specific headers (connection, keep-alive,
transfer-encoding, upgrade, proxy-connection) reset the stream
(RFC 9113 §8.2.2). te is accepted only as trailers.:path goes through the same normaliser and limits.max_url_bytes cap
once the h2 crate has accepted it: a raw space, backtick, < or > in
:path resets the stream before roxy sees it, with no parse_error
event. :authority must equal the CONNECT authority; a host header, if
present, must equal :authority.limits.h2_max_concurrent_streams and limits.h2_max_header_list_bytes
cap streams per connection and header bytes per stream.
CONTINUATION-flood and rapid-reset defences come from the h2 crate.The first stream must open within limits.header_timeout; between
requests the connection may idle for limits.idle_timeout.
79.title: HTTP/2 requests

80.text:
Applied to the request target, for matching and forwarding alike. The path starts with / and contains pchar and /, with well-formed
percent-encodings. [ ] { } | ^ and ` are percent-encoded rather
than rejected (/a|b becomes /a%7Cb). Space, control bytes, ",
<, >, \ and non-ASCII are rejected.Percent-encoded unreserved characters (A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~) are
decoded; other encodings stay (%2F stays %2F).Hex digits in the remaining encodings are upper-cased.Dot segments (including ones %2E-encoded before step 2) are removed
per RFC 3986 §5.2.4. A path that climbs above the root is rejected.An empty path becomes /.The query is validated the same way and its hex upper-cased. /, ?,
[ and ] are also allowed raw; { } | ^ and ` are
percent-encoded; nothing is decoded. It is parsed into pairs for
matching only.A fragment in an HTTP/1.1 target is rejected. The h2 crate drops a
fragment from an HTTP/2 :path before roxy sees it.The host is lower-cased; IDNA labels must already be A-labels (xn--),
raw Unicode is rejected; the port is made explicit; a trailing dot is
removed.
80.title: URL normalisation

81.text:
HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1, whichever ALPN negotiates. HTTP/2 takes the
pseudo-headers from the canonical fields and drops host for
:authority. HTTP/1.1: METHOD <origin-form path[?query]> HTTP/1.1;host first, then the headers in canonical order, lowercase;content-length when known, otherwise clean chunked with no
extensions, never both; a body with trailers fails instead;connection management by roxy's pool; no client hop-by-hop field
survives. Changes from rules and addons are applied to the canonical model before
serialisation and pass the same validation: a header value with a CRLF
denies the flow.
81.title: Upstream serialisation

82.text:
Upstreams are trusted (threat model). hyper parses
the response and roxy builds a CanonicalResponse: Status and headers are kept, names lower-cased; Set-Cookie and
WWW-Authenticate stay separate fields.Hop-by-hop fields are stripped and the framing regenerated:
content-length when known, otherwise clean chunked (HTTP/1.1) or DATA
frames (HTTP/2), with the origin's trailers after the body
(trailers). Responses to HEAD, and 1xx,
204 and 304, carry no body. Empty non-final DATA frames are never
sent upstream.limits.max_response_body_bytes (1 GiB) caps the body.
limits.response_header_timeout (15 m) starts once the request body has
been sent; while it is still being sent, the exchange fails (504) only
if the upstream stops taking it for twice limits.body_idle_timeout.The upstream may pause up to limits.response_body_idle_timeout (30 m)
between parts of the body; longer ends the exchange (response_error,
reason response_body_timeout): close on HTTP/1.1, CANCEL on HTTP/2,
or a 504 while rules are still reading the body and nothing has been
sent.A client that closes while roxy waits for the next part of the body ends
the exchange at once on both versions: the body is dropped, releasing the
upstream and any service streams; a part already there is still written.
On HTTP/1.1 a client that shut down only its sending side counts as gone.Redirects are forwarded, not followed. Encoded bodies pass through
untouched (below).
82.title: Responses

83.text:
roxy decodes content-encoding to inspect a body, never to forward it:
body.text and response.body.text see the decoded text
(body rules); the bytes forwarded
are the bytes received. The one exception is addons: bodies are decoded at
the edge of the stack and forwarded decoded
(content codings for addons). codingformatgzip, x-gzipRFC 1952; several members in a row are one bodydeflatezlib format (RFC 1950), as RFC 9110 defines it; raw deflate is refusedbrRFC 7932, the window the stream declares (up to 16 MiB)zstdRFC 8878, window at most 8 MiB (RFC 9659) Stacked codings are undone in reverse order; identity is ignored; at
most 4 codings, more is refused.An empty body is empty whatever its coding.Decoding is strict: truncated data, a bad checksum, or bytes after the
end of the stream make the body undecodable.Decoders work in bounded steps (a highly compressed body costs time, not
memory); each decoder's window is charged to the
buffer budget before it is allocated.
The decoded size counts against the same cap as the body as sent. http.strip_accept_encoding (default false) removes accept-encoding from
every request as roxy reads it, so origins answer uncompressed. Addons,
rules and the flow log see the request without it.
83.title: Content codings

84.text:
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
content-type: application/json
cache-control: no-store
x-roxy-rule: <rule id>
connection: close

{"error":"blocked by roxy","rule":"<rule id>","flow":"<flow id>"} Every refusal roxy originates has this body: refusalstatusrulea rule denies403, or the rule's deny.statusthe rule idthe process is quarantined403_quarantinedaddress floor403_address_policyunavailable policy input503_fail_closedfailed addon layer503layer:<name>upstream failure502 (504 for a timeout)none The body names the rule and the flow, never why: the reason code
(dns_failed, connect_failed, metric_table_full, ...) is in the flow
log only. A request roxy cannot parse is refused with a different body, before any
rule has seen it: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
content-type: application/json
connection: close

{"error":"rejected by roxy","reason":"cl_and_te"} reason is the parse_error code (rejection rules),
which describes the request's syntax and says nothing about policy. The
status is 400, or the closer one the code has (413, 414, 431, ...);
on HTTP/2 the stream is reset instead. A rule sets the status and message with deny: { status: 451, message:
"..." }. After a deny the connection is closed (connection: close on
HTTP/1.1, GOAWAY on HTTP/2) unless the rule says deny: { close: false
}. On HTTP/1.1 a kept-alive connection discards up to 1 MiB of the
refused body before the next request, and is closed instead beyond that; a
closing response lingers for up to 1 s, discarding up to 1 MiB, so the
client reads the response rather than a reset. After an upstream failure
(502, 504) the connection stays open on both versions.
84.title: Deny responses

85.text:
The protocol between a roxy node (a roxy process in node mode) and its
control plane (any server implementing these four operations). The contract
is
spec/node-protocol/v1/openapi.yaml:
the example bodies here are checked against its schemas in CI and titled
with the schema each satisfies. A node enrols once with a bootstrap token and receives a node token, then
authenticates with it to poll for its lease, ship its flow log and renew
the token. The lease is the whole policy: a rendered roxy.yaml, the
secret values it names, and how long it is good for. An expired lease
denies everything. The control plane never pushes; the node polls.
85.title: Node protocol

86.text:
HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TLS; all paths start with /roxy/v1/. Bodies
are JSON, Content-Type: application/json; unknown fields are ignored by
both sides. The node's User-Agent is roxy/<roxy_version>.Every request carries Authorization: Bearer <token>: the enrolment
token at enrolment, the node token everywhere else. The node presents no
client certificate, so the control plane can sit behind any TLS
terminator; a token only ever travels inside the server's TLS. A request
other than enrolment whose token the server does not recognise is
answered 401.Bootstrap material, given out of band: the control plane URL, an
enrolment token, and optionally a PEM bundle of CA certificates to verify
the control plane with (otherwise the system roots).
86.title: Transport

87.text:
Every non-2xx response carries an error body: error is a stable code,
message is for humans, and a 426 adds missing
(unsupported versions). A
node acts on the status code, not the body. {"error": "invalid_token", "message": "enrolment token not recognised"} statusmeaningnode behaviour400malformed request; error says howlogged apart from a 401; retrying cannot help. Enrolment: retry with backoff for two minutes, then exit non-zero. Renewal: stop renewing. Lease: log once per outcome change, keep polling and let the lease run down. A flow batch is the exception (flow upload)401at enrolment: the token was not accepted. Elsewhere: the node token is not recognised (never issued, expired or forgotten)enrolment: retry with backoff for two minutes (a new token may not have reached every replica), then exit non-zero. Renewal: log once per run of them and retry with backoff under the current token (the replica answering may not yet know the token the last renewal issued). Lease: log once per outcome change, keep polling and let the lease run down. Flows: retry the batch with backoff, as a failure. Never re-enrol unasked: re-enrolment is an operator action410the node is revoked; definite and terminalat enrolment: exit non-zero at once. Elsewhere: expire the lease at once (deny everything, clear the secrets), stop polling, keep /healthz up and /readyz not ready, and offer what is spooled to /flows for up to thirty seconds426the server will not serve this node's protocol_version or roxy_versionenrolment: exit non-zero at once. Renewal: stop renewing. Lease: treat as 5xx; log the missing list distinctly507flow quota exhaustedstop shipping until a lease with a new lease_id arrives (flow upload)5xx, timeout, connection or TLS errorthe control plane is unavailableretry with backoff; the lease runs down
87.title: Errors

88.title: Enrol

89.text:
POST /roxy/v1/renew with the node token and the enrol body; the response
has the enrolment response's shape, with node_id unchanged and a fresh
token. The server keeps accepting the old token until its own
not_after, so a renewal that has reached one replica but not another
cannot lock the node out; the node switches to the new token on receipt
and replaces the one in its state directory. 5xx, timeout, connection and TLS errors are retried with backoff, and so
is a 401: the replica answering may not yet know the token the last
renewal issued, so the node keeps trying under the token it has, logging
once per run of them. 410 is terminal; a 426 or other 4xx is logged
once and ends renewal, and the token serves until its not_after. Once it
expires the node exits non-zero with an error naming the remedy (a new
enrolment token and an empty state dir), as it does on a start whose
stored token has already
expired: no control plane recognises the token, so nothing short of
re-enrolment recovers the node.
89.title: Renew

90.title: Lease

91.text:
{
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "valid_for_seconds": 900,
  "refresh_after_seconds": 300,
  "config": "version: 1\nlisteners:\n  - name: proxy\n    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080\nsecrets:\n  github: { lease: true }\nrules:\n  - id: github\n    when: host == \"api.github.com\"\n    then: [allow]\n",
  "secrets": {
    "github": "ghp_example"
  },
  "state_epoch": "2026-10-06T09:00:00Z",
  "flow": {
    "ship": true,
    "batch_max_bytes": 1048576,
    "flush_interval_seconds": 5,
    "spool_high_water_bytes": 67108864,
    "on_high_water": "hold"
  },
  "quarantine": {
    "release": ["q-01J9ZB7QX4R2M8K3N5P6T7V8W9"]
  }
} fieldmeaninglease_idopaque; changes whenever any other field changes. The node reports it on every poll and quotes it in flow batchesvalid_for_secondsa duration, not an instant: the node sets valid_until = sent_at + valid_for_seconds from its own clock, sent_at being just before it sent the request, so a slow answer shortens the lease and clock skew has no effect. The server's clock is never usedrefresh_after_secondswhen to poll next, counted the same way; leave room for several retries before valid_for_seconds runs out (a third of it is reasonable). The node never polls later than halfway through the leaseconfiga complete roxy.yaml as a string, with no secret values: every secrets: entry the lease supplies is name: { lease: true }secretseach secret name the config declares, to its value, a UTF-8 string. The node reads a missing map as empty, which refuses the lease if the config declares any lease: true secretstate_epochopaque. When it differs from the previous lease's, the node clears every rule set_state entry and every metric window before applying the lease (how a control plane lifts a lockout a rule imposed with set_state); unchanged, state survives a config change. The first lease sets it without clearing anythingflowflow upload settings. ship: false turns shipping off; the other fields are still required. on_high_water is hold (apply roxy's backpressure to traffic when the spool is full) or spool (drop the oldest spooled events, logging once)quarantinereleases of the node's quarantine. release lists incident ids the control plane has released; the node lifts its quarantine when the quarantine.id it reports is among them, and ignores any other id, so a release decided before a later trip lifts nothing. Ids may stay listed indefinitely. Orthogonal to the policy: the rest of the lease is applied whether or not the node is quarantined, so the policy is current the moment the quarantine lifts. Optional; a server that has released nothing leaves it outinterception_careserved; a v1 server does not send it and a v1 node ignores it (the node accepts any value here, whatever the schema says) The node applies only what differs from what it holds: a changed config
rebuilds the policy (the atomic snapshot swap of a file reload); changed
secrets alone swap the in-memory secret map and update the redactor,
leaving rules, addons and upstream pools alone; neither changed only moves
valid_until. A lease is applied in full or not at all: a config that
roxy check would reject, or a secrets map missing a name the config
declares, is logged and discarded, and the node keeps the lease it has. A
node without a lease denies everything and reports not ready.
91.title: Lease body

92.text:
A node reports protocol_version and roxy_version at enrolment, renewal
and every lease fetch. A server that does not speak the protocol version,
or will not serve nodes below some roxy release, answers 426 naming what
the node lacks: {"error": "unsupported", "message": "roxy 0.1.0 is below this server's floor of 0.2.0", "missing": ["roxy_version:0.2.0"]} There is no other capability negotiation: the node parses config
strictly, so a lease using something it does not understand fails to load,
and the lease_id on its next poll shows the server it was not applied.
92.title: Unsupported versions

93.text:
POST /roxy/v1/flows with the node token. The body may be gzip
compressed, signalled with Content-Encoding: gzip. {
  "node_id": "node-7f3a9c",
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "seq_first": 1042,
  "events": [
    {"seq": 1042, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.123Z", "event": "request", "flow": "01J9Z8", "decision": "deny", "terminal_rule": "_default"},
    {"seq": 1043, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.410Z", "event": "log", "flow": "01J9Z9", "rule": "audit"}
  ]
} fieldmeaningnode_idmust match the node the token names, or the answer is 400 node_mismatchlease_idthe lease in force when the batch was assembled; any lease id issued to the node is acceptedseq_firstthe seq of the first event; events are consecutive and in order from it, or the server answers 400eventsflow log records with seq added: a per-node counter that increases by one per shipped event, persisted in the state directory in blocks so it keeps increasing across restarts (a restart skips to the end of the last reservation, at most two blocks of 1024) A batch is at most the lease's batch_max_bytes (the JSON before
compression); the node flushes when that is reached or
flush_interval_seconds has passed since the first unsent event. A server
that refuses a batch within the size it stated is treated as 5xx. {"acked_through": 1043} Delivery is at least once: the server stores the batch, deduplicating on
(node_id, seq), and answers 200 with the highest seq it has stored
for the node; the node drops spooled events at or below acked_through. A
gap within one run means events were dropped (spool mode at the high
water): a server-side alert, not a protocol error. Restarts and ship:
false also leave gaps. responsenode behaviour400 (node_mismatch, a lease_id the server never issued, events not consecutive)logged apart from an outage; the batch is unshipped audit and stays spooled, so under hold traffic stalls until the control plane accepts it507log once and apply on_high_water to what accumulates until a new lease arrives; the control plane is expected to revoke the node or issue it a new lease410shipping stops, and so does the drain that follows a 410 on the lease: a control plane that wants a revoked node's last events keeps accepting its batches401, 5xxas in the errors table
93.title: Flow upload

94.text:
Metrics count exchanges or bytes over a sliding window; state is a bounded
key/value store written with set_state and read as state["key"].
94.title: Rate limits and state

95.text:
Defined once, compared in rules (metric.<id> >= 30). metrics:
  - id: <string>
    count: requests | request_bytes | response_bytes | errors | denied | unique(<field>)
    where: <expr>        # admission values only, no tags: whether it counts
    key: [<field>, ...]  # scalar admission fields; omitted = one global series
    window: <duration>   # omitted = cumulative since start; 0 is a compile error
    max_keys: <n>        # series this metric alone may hold; omitted = limits.max_metric_keys Windows slide in 60 fixed buckets (1-second resolution for 1m). The
store keeps 60 complete buckets plus the current partial one, so a value
may include events up to one bucket older than the window: a limit trips
slightly early, never late. unique is a HyperLogLog sketch per bucket.where may read admission fields, header[..], query[..],
state[..], body.text and metrics; not tag[..] (counted outside the
rules, a tag would always read false). key and the unique(..)
field take scalar admission fields only (client.ip, host, tls.sni, ...),
not header[..] or other indexed values. Anything else is a compile
error.Nullable keys. A flow whose key field is null is denied
(_fail_closed). A key or unique(..) field nullable on an ordinary flow
(tls.sni, tls.alpn, tls.version on plaintext; query.raw without a
query; body.size when chunked) must be guarded in where (tls.sni !=
null, or an and with that as a top-level term) or the metric does not
compile; such flows are not counted. A rule reading the metric needs the
same guard (tls.sni != null and metric.by_sni > 30).When counts move. requests and denied are read before the
forwarding decision and incremented after it (denied flows count), so
metric.x >= 30 denies the 31st request. request_bytes and
response_bytes grow as bytes stream: a deny or quarantine reading them
is re-checked in flight and stops the exchange that crosses the limit; a
chunk is counted before it is checked, so a budget overcounts by at most
one chunk. errors count when the exchange ends.Bounds (never evict):
limits.max_metric_keys (100 000) series across all metrics; each
metric's max_keys (at most the shared limit, its default); and,
approximately, limits.max_metric_bytes (256 MiB, at most 64 GiB; a
series is charged for key, buckets and a fixed overhead). A flow needing
a new series when any is exhausted is denied (_fail_closed, reason
metric_table_full); a byte metric that cannot record a chunk mid-stream
stops the exchange the same way. Series are reclaimed only once their
window has fully expired.Reload. A metric keeps its series when its id, count, where,
key and window are unchanged (where compared as written); any other
change to it starts it empty, and a removed metric's series are dropped
silently. Changing only max_keys carries over. Carried series may
exceed a lowered max_metric_keys or max_keys until they expire (new
series refused meanwhile), but never the byte budget: a series that does
not fit is dropped with a warning.
95.title: Metrics

96.text:
host, path, url and query.raw are chosen by the client per
request, and denied flows count, so a metric keyed on one with
no where fills with as many series as the client sends, without one
request being allowed; then every flow needing a new series is denied
(metric_table_full) until series expire. Bound the key with a finite
where: metrics:
  - id: github_requests
    count: requests
    where: host in ["api.github.com", "github.com"]
    key: [host]
    window: 1m client.ip is bounded by who can reach the proxy; behind a load balancer
it is each client's own address only with the listener's forwarded_for
(HTTP). roxy check warns when a
metric keys on any of the four fields above with no where. host under
"github.com" does not bound host: subdomains are client-chosen too. For
path, url and query.raw a where on host limits
whose values count, not how many; give such a metric a where that
enumerates the values it keys on, or its own max_keys so filling it
refuses new series in that metric alone. unique(..) fields are not keys:
they feed a bounded sketch inside a series and create none.
96.title: Key cardinality

97.text:
A bounded key/value map with per-entry TTL: the rule's ttl, or one hour;
ttl: 0 is a compile error. At most limits.max_state_entries (100 000)
stored entries, expired ones included until they are purged (every 1024
writes, and at most every 100 ms when a new key meets a full table); a new
key when full denies the flow (503, _fail_closed, reason
state_unavailable). State is shared across flows, so reads are
order-dependent: state["key"] sees what earlier flows wrote and, within
a flow, the set_state of rules above the reader. A WASM layer reads and
writes the same store (host services).
97.title: State

98.text:
secrets: maps names to sources. ${secret:name} in an admission rule's
set_header value or sign credentials, or an addon endpoint's headers,
injects the value; the client holds only a placeholder. A reference
anywhere else is a compile error. secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline (`\n` or `\r\n`) stripped; warns if group or world can read it
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control-plane lease

rules:
  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # replaces whatever the client sent
      - allow Exactly one of env, file, lease: true; {}, null, a bare word
and lease: false are parse errors.env and file resolve at start and on reload; missing or empty is
fatal. roxy check and roxy rule test do not resolve secrets.At evaluation, a missing secret fails closed (_fail_closed, reason
secret_missing); one that is not a valid header value, secret_invalid.Injected values are redacted from the flow log and capture heads.A redirect in a matching rule sends the request, injected values
included, to the redirect target: a secret's set_header rule should
not match a request another rule redirects elsewhere.
98.title: Secrets

99.text:
sign: { aws_sigv4: ... }, an admission-rule action, signs the forwarded request
with AWS Signature Version 4, so a client holding placeholder credentials
reaches AWS with a real signature. Credential fields take ${secret:name} as
set_header does; session_token is optional. secrets:
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }
  aws_token: { env: AWS_SESSION_TOKEN }

rules:
  - id: bedrock
    when: host under "bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com" and scheme == "https"
    then:
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
            session_token: "${secret:aws_token}"   # optional
      - allow Signed: the request as forwarded, after every other admission effect
(set_header, rewrite_path, redirect, ...) whatever sign's
position in then. The client's authorization, x-amz-date,
x-amz-security-token and x-amz-content-sha256 are removed first.
host is signed as sent upstream. Not signed: connection,
transfer-encoding, content-length, accept-encoding, te,
trailer, upgrade, keep-alive, proxy-connection (re-serialised by
roxy), user-agent, x-amzn-trace-id (changed by intermediaries).
Every other header is. A non-UTF-8 header value (obs-text, under
http.allow_obs_text) is refused with 400 (terminal_rule: _sign,
reason: sign_header_invalid).service is the signing name (bedrock, s3, execute-api, ...).
s3, s3-control and s3-outposts use the S3 variant: path encoded
once, not normalised; payload hash sent as x-amz-content-sha256.Presigned: a request whose query carries X-Amz-Signature goes out
under the client's query signature, its authorization and x-amz-*
signature headers stripped, no signature of roxy's; mutations records
sign:presigned. It reaches AWS as whoever signed the URL; the rule's
host and path conditions bound where it may go.Two matching rules that both sign fail closed (sign_conflict).Body: buffered up to limits.max_sign_body_bytes (100 MiB) for the
payload hash; over that, declared or chunked, is 413 (terminal_rule:
_sign, reason: sign_body_too_large) and the connection closed.
unsigned_payload: true signs UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD and streams the body;
only S3 accepts it, so it is a config error with any other service.Tools: mutations records sign:aws_sigv4; the credentials are
redacted like any secret. roxy rule test shows sign aws_sigv4
service=... region=... without computing a signature; roxy check
validates the block.
